answers.label: Q.1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Knowledge and skills across the world are changing fast, so education must change to keep up.
answers.solution: 'A major change in terms of knowledge globally' means that what people need to know, and the skills they need, are changing very fast all over the world (new technology, new kinds of jobs, new ideas). India's education system has to change too, so that its students can keep pace with the rest of the world. This is why the old 1986 policy was replaced by NEP 2020.

answers.label: Q.1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: Making schooling available to every child from pre-school up to the secondary level (100% GER by 2030).
answers.solution: It means bringing every child of the right age into school, from pre-school right up to the secondary level, so that no child is left out. The passage says the policy aims at a 100% Gross Enrollment Ratio in schooling by 2030.

answers.label: Q.1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: By opening Indian higher education to foreign universities and starting a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programme with exit options (and making all colleges multidisciplinary by 2040).
answers.solution:
The policy will try to make India a global knowledge superpower in these ways:
1. It opens Indian higher education to foreign universities.
2. It introduces a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programme with several exit options.
3. It aims to make all universities and colleges multidisciplinary by 2040.
The passage says, 'Thus, this new policy will strive to make the country a global knowledge superpower.'

answers.label: Q.1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Board exams of classes 10 and 12 will be made easier; they will test core competencies instead of memorization of facts; students can take the exam twice.
answers.solution:
Testing will change in three ways:
1. The board exams of classes 10 and 12 will be made easier.
2. The exams will test core competencies (real understanding and skills) instead of mere memorization of facts.
3. All students will be allowed to take the exam twice.

answers.label: Q.1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Educational streams are the academic subjects studied for knowledge (science, arts, commerce); vocational streams train students in practical job skills. The policy removes the sharp line between them, starting vocational education with an internship from class 6.
answers.solution: Educational (academic) streams are the regular subjects such as science, commerce and the arts, studied mainly for knowledge. Vocational streams teach practical skills for a job or trade. The passage says the policy will remove any sharp separation between the two, and vocational education will begin in class 6 with an internship.

answers.label: Q.1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: Admission to foreign universities will probably make the education system expensive.
answers.solution: The passage says NEP 2020 can make the education system expensive because higher education is being opened to foreign universities, and admission to such universities will probably cost a lot more.

answers.label: Q.1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: Without enough skilled teachers, the policy will face practical problems in being carried out, especially in elementary education, so it may not succeed.
answers.solution: There is already a lack of skilled teachers in elementary education. So the new system will face practical problems when it is put into action at that level. If there are not enough good teachers to carry out the new ideas, the policy cannot succeed as planned.

answers.label: Q.1(h)
answers.finalAnswer: Skilled teachers may leave Indian institutions and migrate to the foreign universities (an exodus of teachers), making the shortage at home worse.
answers.solution:
The passage calls this 'the exodus of teachers'. When foreign universities are opened to Indian students, our skilled teachers will be attracted to them and will migrate to those universities. India will then lose many of its best teachers, and the shortage of skilled teachers in our own schools and colleges will become worse.

(The question as printed says 'by the success of NEP2020'; the passage presents this as a drawback of the policy, so the answer is taken from that part.)

answers.label: Q.1(i)
answers.finalAnswer: Its implementation.
answers.solution: The proper implementation of the policy. The passage says, 'the implementation of this policy will greatly determine its success.'

answers.label: Q.1(j)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) single-disciplinary (unidisciplinary); (ii) influx
answers.solution:
(i) Multidisciplinary (involving many subjects): its opposite is single-disciplinary (also called unidisciplinary), involving only one subject.
(ii) Exodus (a large number of people leaving a place): its opposite is influx, a large number of people coming into a place.

answers.label: Q.2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Holding the poem up to the light like a colour slide; tying the poem to a chair with rope and torturing a confession out of it.
answers.solution:
Two images that stand out are:
1. Holding a poem up to the light 'like a color slide', looking at it closely and calmly to enjoy it.
2. Tying the poem 'to a chair with rope' and beating it with a hose to 'torture a confession out of it'.
The first shows how the poet wants poems to be read; the second shows how the students actually treat them. (Other good images: pressing an ear against the poem's hive, dropping a mouse into a poem, waterskiing across its surface.)

answers.label: Q.2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: Amusement mixed with a little sadness: the playful images are funny, but it is sad that the students only want to force out a meaning instead of enjoying the poem.
answers.solution: The poem makes me smile at first, because the images are playful and funny, such as dropping a mouse into a poem or waterskiing across it. By the end I feel a little sad, because the students do not enjoy the poem at all; they only want to beat a 'meaning' out of it. I choose this mix of amusement and sadness because the poem itself moves from fun and freedom in the first part to violence in the last lines.

answers.label: Q.2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Simile: 'hold it up to the light / like a color slide'; Metaphor/personification: 'tie the poem to a chair with rope / and torture a confession out of it'.
answers.solution:
1. Simile: 'and hold it up to the light / like a color slide'. The poem is compared to a colour slide using 'like'.
2. Personification (an extended metaphor): 'tie the poem to a chair with rope / and torture a confession out of it'. The poem is treated like a prisoner who can be tied up and made to confess.
(Also correct: metaphor in 'press an ear against its hive', where the poem is a beehive full of life and sound.)

answers.label: Q.2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: How poetry should be read: a poem should be explored and enjoyed with curiosity, not forced to give up one fixed meaning.
answers.solution: The theme is the right way to read and enjoy poetry. The teacher wants students to explore a poem freely, look at it, listen to it, move around inside it and enjoy it. The students, however, only want to find out 'what it really means' and treat the poem roughly. The poem contrasts these two ways of reading to show that hunting for one hidden meaning spoils the joy of poetry.

answers.label: Q.2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Forcing the poem to give up its 'real meaning' by harsh analysis, like a prisoner forced to confess.
answers.solution: To 'torture a confession' out of someone is to force a prisoner to admit something by hurting him. In the poem it means the students analyse the poem harshly and mechanically, trying to force it to tell them its one 'real meaning', instead of enjoying and exploring it.

answers.label: Q.2(f)
answers.finalAnswer: To explore and enjoy the poem freely, experiencing it rather than hunting for a fixed meaning.
answers.solution: According to the poet, the real goal of reading poetry is to explore and enjoy a poem: to look at it, listen to it, move around inside it and have fun with it, as the images of the colour slide, the hive and the waterskiing show. It is not to force one fixed meaning out of it.

answers.label: Q.3
answers.solution:
Mangalam Vihar Colony
Kolkata

15 December 2022

The Editor
The Hindu
Chennai

Subject: Commercialization of our festivals

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to express my deep concern about the way our festivals are being turned into business events.

Festivals such as Diwali, Durga Puja, Eid and Christmas were meant to bring families and neighbours together in prayer, joy and sharing. Today, however, they have become occasions for shopping and showing off. For weeks before a festival, advertisements tell us that we must buy new phones, clothes and gifts to celebrate properly. Pandals compete with one another to look bigger and costlier, and sponsors' banners are often larger than the idol of the goddess. Sweets are bought in fancy boxes instead of being made at home with love.

This has harmful effects. Poor families feel ashamed when they cannot spend as much as others. Children begin to think that a festival means only gifts and money. The prayers, the stories and the values behind each festival are forgotten. Heavy spending on lights and crackers also adds to noise and air pollution.

I request citizens to celebrate simply and sincerely, and I urge puja committees and shopkeepers to remember the real spirit of our festivals. Schools too can teach students the true meaning behind each celebration.

I hope you will publish this letter so that more people think about this issue.

Yours faithfully,
Shalini
Resident, Mangalam Vihar Colony

answers.label: Q.4
answers.solution:
Global Citizens or Nationalists?

Some people complain that schools today teach students to be global citizens instead of teaching them to love their nation. I believe this is a false choice. A good school should do both, and most schools already do.

A global citizen is a person who understands that problems such as climate change, disease and poverty affect the whole world, and who respects people of every country, religion and culture. In today's connected world, our students will study, work and trade with people from many nations. They must learn foreign languages, modern science and respect for others.

However, a person who has no roots is like a tree without soil. Students must also know India's history, its freedom struggle, its Constitution and its rich culture. Singing the national anthem with pride, respecting our soldiers and serving our own community are lessons no school should drop.

In fact, true nationalism and global citizenship support each other. An Indian who knows the world can serve India better, and an Indian who loves India can represent it proudly abroad. Leaders such as Swami Vivekananda and Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam were deeply Indian and respected across the world.

Therefore, schools should not choose one over the other. They should produce proud Indians who are also responsible citizens of the world.

answers.label: Q.5
answers.solution:
Anxiety among Children
By Shalini, Class VIII

We often think that worry belongs only to adults. Yet many children today feel anxious. A tight stomach before a test, sleepless nights before results, or fear of speaking in class are all signs of anxiety.

What causes it?
The biggest cause is pressure to perform. Children are compared with cousins, classmates and toppers. Long hours of tuition leave little time to play. Social media adds to the problem, because everyone else seems happier and more successful online. Problems at home, bullying at school and fear of the future also make children worried.

How does it affect us?
An anxious child may lose appetite, have headaches, stay alone or lose interest in hobbies. Some children become angry; others become silent. Anxiety also lowers marks, because a worried mind cannot concentrate.

What can we do?
First, children must talk about their feelings to a parent, teacher or friend. Sharing a worry makes it smaller. Second, regular exercise, enough sleep and healthy food keep both the body and the mind strong. Third, we should limit screen time. Parents and teachers can help by praising effort rather than only marks and by listening patiently. Schools can arrange counsellors and fun activities that relieve stress.

Conclusion
Anxiety is not a weakness; it is a signal that a child needs help and care. With understanding at home and support at school, every child can face challenges with a calm and confident mind.

answers.label: Q.6
answers.solution:
Popular Culture and the Global Citizen

Today K-pop songs from South Korea are played in Indian homes, and young people across the world dance to Bollywood music. Popular culture, which includes music, films, fashion, food and games, has become a bridge between nations. When young people enjoy the songs or shows of another country, they become curious about its language, history and way of life. This curiosity grows into respect, and respect is the first quality of a global citizen. Fans from many countries meet online, share ideas and form friendships across borders. Popular culture also lets India share its own art with the world, as yoga, Indian food and our films have shown. However, we must enjoy foreign culture wisely, without blindly copying it or forgetting our own traditions. Used well, popular culture helps us understand others, value our own roots and live as responsible citizens of one world.

answers.label: Q.7
answers.solution:
A story based on the picture.

The Winning Pass

Arjun had been the fastest runner in his class until a road accident took away the use of his legs. For months after he came home from hospital in a wheelchair, he refused to go out. He believed his days of sport were over.

One evening his coach, Mr Mehta, came to see him. 'There is a wheelchair basketball team at the sports centre,' he said. 'They need a sharp player. Will you come and watch?'

Arjun went unwillingly. In the hall he saw boys like him racing across the court in their wheelchairs, turning quickly, passing the ball and laughing loudly. Nobody looked sad. One boy waved at him to join.

The first few days were hard. His arms ached from pushing the wheels, and the ball often slipped from his hands. But his teammates cheered every small improvement, and slowly his speed and aim got better.

Three months later his team played in the district tournament. In the last minute the score was level. Arjun held the ball, saw his friend free near the basket and made a perfect pass. The basket was scored and the hall burst into cheers.

That night Arjun wrote in his diary: 'I lost the use of my legs, but I have not lost my spirit.' The picture of those boys in wheelchairs reminds us that a disability can limit the body, but never a determined mind.

answers.label: Q.8
answers.finalAnswer: (iii); (iii); (iv); (i); (ii)
answers.solution:
(a) Error in part (iii): 'one of the least important persons'. After 'one of the', the noun must be plural.
(b) Error in part (iii): 'Hardly had the teacher left the room when the pupils started enjoying.' 'Hardly' is followed by 'when', not 'than'.
(c) No error (iv). The sentence is acceptable as it stands.
(d) Error in part (i): 'Her walking hurriedly'. A possessive (her), not 'she', is used before a gerund.
(e) Error in part (ii): 'he did not want to take action'. 'Want' is followed by the infinitive, not '-ing'. (Part (iii) should also read 'reporter's version', but the main grammatical error is in part (ii).)

Note: the printed part labels are misnumbered in (a) and (b): in (a) 'no error' is labelled (ii) instead of (iv), and in (b) the first part is labelled (ii) instead of (i). The answers above use the intended labels (i) to (iv).

answers.label: Q.9
answers.finalAnswer: (a) Selfish; (b) Frequently; (c) Satiety; (d) in: in: of; (e) Torrential; (f) Rubric; (g) Gender Dynamics; (h) 1c:2a:3d:4b; (i) Corrupted; (j) Array; (k) Expatia; (l) as the magic-bullet solution to disposing of otherwise; (m) PSQR; (n) asked us, "Where were all of you last night?"; (o) simultaneous
answers.solution:
(a) (i) Selfish. 'Benevolent' means kind and generous; 'but' shows the opposite.
(b) (ii) Frequently: 'I visit my village frequently to see my aged grandparents.'
(c) Satiety (the third option): 'There is no satiety in the pursuit of knowledge.' Satiety is the noun meaning 'the state of being fully satisfied'. (The options are misprinted: the third and fourth are both labelled (iii).)
(d) (iv) in: in: of: 'organized in Jaipur, one of the most affluent towns in Rajasthan and known as the pink city of the country.' (The stem should read 'towns'.)
(e) (iii) Torrential: very heavy rain.
(f) (iv) Rubric: a scoring guide for assessing student work.
(g) (i) Gender Dynamics.
(h) (iii) 1c:2a:3d:4b. Absolute = complete, Obsolete = archaic, Absolve = acquit, Obstinate = stubborn.
(i) (iv) Corrupted. 'Debased' means lowered in quality or value.
(j) (iv) Array.
(k) (ii) Expatia is spelt wrongly; the word is 'expatiate'.
(l) (i) 'as the magic-bullet solution to disposing of otherwise'. We 'dispose of' something, and 'solution to' is the correct form.
(m) (ii) PSQR: Uranus married Gaia (P), they had twelve children, the Titans (S), he hid the children inside their mother (Q), and Gaia hated him for this (R).
(n) (iii) asked us, "Where were all of you last night?" A question in direct speech ends with a question mark, and 'that' is not used before quoted words.
(o) (ii) simultaneous.

answers.label: Q.10
answers.finalAnswer: (a) (ii) won't be felt / will have been exhausted; (b) (i) had learnt / started; (c) (iii) have tried; (d) (ii) have estimated / is; (e) (iii) will have / have finished; (f) (i) hasn't told / won't be coming; (g) (ii) retired / had been; (h) (iv) finished / had arrived; (i) (iv) have visited / moved; (j) (iii) were / is
answers.solution:
(a) (ii) 'won't be felt till next week, by which time present stocks will have been exhausted': future, then future perfect for an action complete before a future time.
(b) (i) 'only after she had learnt English that she started': the earlier past action takes the past perfect.
(c) (iii) 'For decades, researchers have tried': 'for decades' up to now needs the present perfect.
(d) (ii) 'We have estimated that this picture is worth': present perfect, and the worth is a present fact.
(e) (iii) 'Next weekend, I will have my proficiency exam, so I have finished more or less 300 questions so far': 'so far' needs the present perfect.
(f) (i) 'He hasn't told his boss that he won't be coming back after his vacation.'
(g) (ii) 'By the time Richard retired from the army, he had been involved in three riots.'
(h) (iv) 'By the time we finished our preparations, most of the participants had arrived': the earlier action takes the past perfect.
(i) (iv) 'I have visited ... many times ever since I moved to Israel a year ago': 'ever since' takes the present perfect with a simple past after it.
(j) (iii) 'where many important people were at one time imprisoned, is today visited by tourists'.

answers.label: Q.11
answers.finalAnswer: (a) for good; (b) takes after; (c) getting along; (d) cut through; (e) get away
answers.solution:
(a) I'm leaving for good this time. ('for good' = for ever)
(b) The child takes after his mother, not his father. ('take after' = resemble)
(c) The new bird is getting along well with the other ones in the cage. ('get along' = have a friendly relationship)
(d) Let's cut through the backyard and jump over the fence. ('cut through' = take a short way across)
(e) The criminal wasn't able to get away with the murder. ('get away with' = escape punishment for)

No options are printed, so other suitable phrases are also correct where they fit the sense (for example 'run across' in (d)).

answers.label: Q.12
answers.finalAnswer: I was asked by Margaret not to forget to meet her the next day.; Though I warned Dev, he ignored me.; It makes no difference which chemical you put into the mixture first; the results will be the same.; Do you know who this pen belongs to?; This is the first time I have seen so many people in this building.; Most of the books had gone from the shelf when we left.
answers.solution:
1. I was asked by Margaret not to forget to meet her the next day.
2. Though I warned Dev, he ignored me.
3. It makes no difference which chemical you put into the mixture first; the results will be the same.
4. Do you know who this pen belongs to? (Or: Do you know whom this pen belongs to?) In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb, and 'does' is dropped. (The instruction is misprinted 'Being' for 'Begin'.)
5. This is the first time I have seen so many people in this building.
6. Most of the books had gone from the shelf when we left. 'Only a few were remaining' means most were no longer there.

answers.label: Q.13
answers.finalAnswer: (a) I told my teacher that I needed his help.; (b) He told me that I was lucky.; (c) The children told me that they would go out in the rain.; (d) The teacher said that the school would remain closed the next day.
answers.solution:
(a) I told my teacher that I needed his (or her) help.
(b) He told me that I was lucky.
(c) The children told me that they would go out in the rain.
(d) The teacher said that the school would remain closed the next day.
Rules: 'said to' becomes 'told'; the reporting verb is in the past, so present becomes past and 'will' becomes 'would'; pronouns change to suit the speaker; 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

answers.label: Q.14
answers.finalAnswer: (a) tiny; (b) careless; (c) retail; (d) produce; (e) accidental
answers.solution:
(a) Immense (very large): tiny (or minute).
(b) Thorough (complete and careful): careless (or superficial).
(c) Wholesale (selling in large quantities): retail.
(d) Consume (use up): produce.
(e) Deliberate (done on purpose): accidental (or unintentional).
